title: Ocular Chemical Injury: A Race Against Time
summary: Ocular chemical injury is an ophthalmologic emergency requiring immediate and aggressive management to preserve vision and prevent severe complications. Understanding the etiology, pathophysiology, and classification is critical for guiding a stepwise approach from initial irrigation to complex surgical reconstruction.

data.title: Ocular Chemical Injury: A Race Against Time
data.summary: Ocular chemical injury is an ophthalmologic emergency requiring immediate and aggressive management to preserve vision and prevent severe complications. Understanding the etiology, pathophysiology, and classification is critical for guiding a stepwise approach from initial irrigation to complex surgical reconstruction.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular chemical injury refers to damage to the ocular surface and adnexa caused by exposure to acidic or alkaline substances. It is a true ophthalmic emergency, potentially leading to severe vision loss, pain, and disfigurement due to rapid tissue destruction, inflammation, and subsequent scarring. Alkali burns are generally more severe than acid burns due to their saponification and deeper penetration capabilities.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: Incidence: Approximately 15-20% of all ocular trauma cases.
Prevalence: More common in young males (16-45 years) due to occupational hazards.
Location: Most commonly occurs at home (e.g., cleaning products) or in industrial/laboratory settings.
Risk Factors: Lack of personal protective equipment (PPE), improper handling of chemicals, workplace accidents, assault, accidental splashing (e.g., battery acid, household cleaners).

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content:
**Alkali Burns:** Rapidly penetrate ocular tissues by saponifying cell membranes and forming hydroxyl ions (OH-) that cause liquefactive necrosis. This allows the alkali to continue penetrating deeper, destroying collagen matrix, extracellular proteoglycans, and cellular components. Effects include stromal hydration, limbal stem cell destruction, ciliary body damage (leading to hypotony), and vascular occlusion. Examples: Ammonia (NH3), lye (NaOH), lime (Ca(OH)2), magnesium hydroxide (Mg(OH)2).

**Acid Burns:** Typically cause coagulative necrosis by precipitating proteins, forming a barrier that often limits further penetration. This is less severe than liquefactive necrosis but can still cause significant damage, especially with strong acids (e.g., hydrofluoric acid). The severity depends on the pH, volume, duration of contact, and buffering capacity of the tissue. Examples: Sulfuric acid (H2SO4), hydrochloric acid (HCl), acetic acid (CH3COOH).

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Severe eye pain
Foreign body sensation
Photophobia
Blepharospasm
Decreased vision
Redness (conjunctival hyperemia)
Tearing (epiphora)
Corneal edema and opacification (white, porcelain-like cornea often indicates severe ischemia)
Conjunctival chemosis
Eyelid swelling (edema)
Symblepharon (adhesion between conjunctiva of lid and globe) in chronic cases

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: Visual Acuity: May range from normal to no light perception.
Eyelids: Edema, erythema, possible necrosis.
Conjunctiva: Hyperemia, chemosis, blanching of limbal vessels (indicating ischemia), necrotic tissue, possible symblepharon.
Cornea: Epithelial defect (stains with fluorescein), haze, stromal edema, ulceration, opacification (ground glass to porcelain white), neovascularization (later stages).
Anterior Chamber: Inflammatory cells (flare and cells), hypopyon, cyclitic membrane, iris atrophy, synechiae.
Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Initially elevated due to inflammation and trabecular meshwork damage; later may be reduced due to ciliary body damage (hypotony).
Fundus: Difficult to visualize in severe cases; optic nerve atrophy (late complication).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: **Immediate pH Measurement** (Crucial!): After initial irrigation, use litmus paper or pH indicator strips to measure conjunctival sac pH. Normal pH is 7.0-7.4. Continue irrigation until pH is normalized for at least 30 minutes after last drop of irrigant.
Step 2: **Visual Acuity Assessment**: Document baseline VA.

Step 3: **Slit Lamp Examination**: Detailed assessment of cornea, conjunctiva, limbus, anterior chamber, and lens. Document extent of epithelial defect (fluorescein stain), limbal ischemia (clock hours of blanching), corneal clarity, and anterior chamber reaction.
Step 4: **Intraocular Pressure (IOP) Measurement**: Using applanation tonometry (if cornea clear enough) or TonoPen.
Step 5: **Fundus Examination**: If media clear enough to rule out posterior segment involvement (rare but possible with very deep penetration).
Step 6: **Photography**: Document initial status and progression.
Step 7: **Ancillary Tests (Later Stage)**: OCT (corneal edema, scarring), corneal topography (irregular astigmatism), anterior segment OCT (limbal stem cell health, symblepharon).

sections.title: 10. Immediate Management & Treatment: The First 30 Minutes
content: Step 1: **IMMEDIATE IRRIGATION (CRITICAL!)**: Do NOT delay for VA or pH measurement. Begin with copious irrigation (1-2 liters/eye) using sterile saline (e.g., Lactated Ringer's solution, normal saline). If sterile solutions are unavailable, tap water is acceptable in the field. Use a Morgan lens if available to facilitate continuous irrigation. Remove any particulate matter (e.g., lime) with a cotton-tipped applicator.

Step 2: **Evert Eyelids**: Ensure thorough irrigation of superior and inferior fornices. Use a topical anesthetic (e.g., proparacaine 0.5% or tetracaine 0.5%) to facilitate examination and irrigation.

Step 3: **Measure pH**: After 5-10 minutes of irrigation, check conjunctival pH. Continue irrigation until pH normalizes (7.0-7.4) and remains stable for at least 30 minutes after discontinuing irrigation. This may require hours of irrigation.
Step 4: **Remove Necrotic Tissue**: Carefully debride any necrotic conjunctival or corneal tissue to prevent further inflammatory stimulus and enhance healing.

sections.title: 10.1 Subsequent Medical Management
content: **Topical Corticosteroids**: Initially high-dose (e.g., Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h to q2h) for severe inflammation. Taper quickly after 7-10 days due to risk of collagenolysis and corneal melting. Consider NSAIDs if steroids contraindicated or for less severe cases (e.g., diclofenac 0.1% or ketorolac 0.4%).

**Topical Antibiotics**: Prophylactic broad-spectrum (e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5%, Gatifloxacin 0.5%, Ofloxacin 0.3%) qid to prevent secondary infection, especially with epithelial defects. Consider fortified antibiotics if infection suspected.
**Cycloplegics**: To reduce ciliary spasm and pain (e.g., Cyclopentolate 1% bid-tid or Atropine 1% bid).

**Aqueous Suppressants**: If IOP is elevated (e.g., topical beta-blockers like Timolol 0.5% bid, alpha-agonists like Brimonidine 0.2% bid, or oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like Acetazolamide 250mg qid). Avoid prostaglandin analogues as they can exacerbate inflammation.
**Lubricants**: Preservative-free artificial tears (q1h-q2h) and lubricating ointments (at night) to promote epithelial healing and comfort.
**Oral Doxycycline**: 50-100mg bid, as a matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) inhibitor, to prevent collagenolysis and corneal melting in severe cases.
**Oral Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid)**: 2g/day, thought to be a cofactor for collagen synthesis and a scavenger of free radicals.
**Autologous Serum Tears/Plasma-Rich Plasma**: Promote epithelial healing and reduce inflammation.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques
content: Step 1: **Debridement of Necrotic Tissue**: Early removal of devitalized conjunctiva and corneal epithelium.

Step 2: **Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT)**: For persistent epithelial defects, corneal ulcers, or significant limbal stem cell damage. Promotes re-epithelialization, reduces inflammation, and inhibits angiogenesis and scarring. Can be done early (PROKERA/PROKERA Slim) or as a patch/graft.
Step 3: **Symblepharon Lysis with Conjunctival Reconstruction**: For severe adhesion between conjunctiva and globe, often using autologous conjunctival grafts, oral mucosal grafts, or AMT.

Step 4: **Limbal Stem Cell Transplantation (LSCT)**: For total limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD) in unilateral cases (autologous contralateral eye) or bilateral cases (allogeneic from living related donor or cadaveric). Techniques include Conjunctival Limbal Autograft (CLAU), Cultivated Limbal Epithelial Transplantation (CLET), or simple limbal epithelial transplantation (SLET).

Step 5: **Keratoplasty**: Penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) or deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) for severe corneal opacification and vision loss. High risk of failure due to inflammation and neovascularization; often preceded by LSCT.
Step 6: **Keratoprosthesis (KPro)**: For end-stage cases with recurrent graft failure and severe LSCD (e.g., Boston Type I or Type II KPro).

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Corneal Complications**: Persistent epithelial defects, corneal ulceration, sterile corneal melts, infectious keratitis, corneal scarring, neovascularization, glaucoma, limbal stem cell deficiency, irregular astigmatism.
**Conjunctival Complications**: Symblepharon, ankyloblepharon (fusion of eyelids), fornix shortening, severe dry eye.

**Intraocular Complications**: Secondary glaucoma (due to trabecular meshwork scarring or peripheral anterior synechiae), hypotony (ciliary body damage), cataract, iris atrophy, phthisis bulbi (end-stage atrophy of the globe).
**Prognosis**: Directly correlated with the extent of limbal ischemia (Roper-Hall/Hughes classification). Grade I-II typically good; Grade III guarded; Grade IV poor.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: ANY chemical exposure to the eye – Initiate irrigation IMMEDIATELY.
White, opaque, or porcelain-like cornea – Indicates severe limbal ischemia and poor prognosis.
Blanching of limbal blood vessels – Critical sign of ischemia (Grade II or higher).
Persistent elevated intraocular pressure despite medical therapy.
Progressive corneal thinning or melting.
Any sign of secondary infection (e.g., new infiltrates, worsening pain/redness).
Inability to achieve or maintain normal conjunctival pH after extensive irrigation.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Alkali burns are generally worse than acid burns due to liquefactive necrosis and deeper penetration.
The pH of the conjunctival fornices is the most critical parameter to monitor during initial management.
Limbal ischemia is the most important prognostic indicator.
Aggressive, prolonged irrigation is the cornerstone of immediate management and directly impacts outcome.
Early intervention with AMT can significantly improve outcomes in moderate to severe burns.
Topical steroids, while reducing inflammation, must be used judiciously and tapered due to the risk of corneal melting.
Oral doxycycline and vitamin C are crucial adjuncts in severe cases to prevent stromal lysis and promote healing.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT)**: Extensive research supports early application of AMT (e.g., PROKERA) for reducing inflammation, promoting epithelial healing, and preventing limbal stem cell damage in moderate-severe burns.

**Limbal Stem Cell Transplantation (LSCT)**: Refinements in techniques like SLET (Simple Limbal Epithelial Transplantation) and CLET (Cultivated Limbal Epithelial Transplantation) have improved success rates for total limbal stem cell deficiency, offering better alternatives to traditional CLAU/conjunctival transplantation.
**Biomaterials and Tissue Engineering**: Development of novel scaffolds and growth factors for ocular surface reconstruction, aiming to create more biocompatible and effective long-term solutions.

**Anti-Inflammatory & Anti-Fibrotic Strategies**: Ongoing research into targeted therapies to modulate the inflammatory response and prevent scar formation, including new MMP inhibitors and anti-VEGF agents for neovascularization.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Pediatric Patients**: Chemical injuries are often accidental (e.g., cleaning products, battery acid). Management is challenging due to poor cooperation. Sedation or general anesthesia may be required for adequate irrigation and examination. Child abuse should always be considered in suspicious cases.
**Contact Lens Wearers**: Instruct patient to remove contact lenses immediately. The lens itself can harbor chemical residue, extending contact time.
**Pregnant Patients**: Avoid medications with known teratogenic effects if possible, but immediate life- and sight-saving treatment takes precedence. Discuss risks vs. benefits.
**Monocular Patients**: Management is even more aggressive given the sole remaining eye.
**Patients with Pre-existing Ocular Surface Disease**: May have worse outcomes due to compromised healing capacity.
